key_claims: Body size predicted lifespan duration in 18 Australian ant species.
Colony size and the size-temperature interaction did not moderate the size-longevity relationship.
A weak but significant size-foraging-rate interaction was detected.
Senescence trajectory was associated with circadian niche, being steepest in matinal species, and was uncorrelated with body mass.
Thermal hazard plateaued above 20 degrees C, with elevated thermal sensitivity in Rhytidoponera above the plateau.
Circadian regime and lineage identity, not body size, emerged as the most climate-relevant axes.
limitations: The study was conducted on 18 Australian ant species, which may not represent all ant species globally.
The circadian regime and lineage identity were strongly collinear, making it difficult to separate their effects.
The study did not measure all potential ecological factors that could influence mortality.
The source is an arXiv preprint and may not have undergone full peer review.
what_not_to_say: Do not claim that body size is the sole predictor of mortality risk in ants.
Do not claim that colony size has no effect on ant longevity, as the study only found no detectable moderating effect.
Do not claim that thermal sensitivity is uniform across all ant species, as Rhytidoponera showed elevated sensitivity.
Do not claim that the study provides causal evidence for the relationships, as it is observational.
Do not claim that the findings apply to all social insects beyond ants.
